Nethinims
nĕth'ĭ-nĭmz
n. pl. (the given ones — temple servants of foreign descent assigned to assist the Levites, and among the first to come back from Babylon)
From Hebrew Nethinim, the passive participle of nathan, to give — literally “the given ones”, those donated to the service of the sanctuary. The KJV adds an English plural to a word already plural in Hebrew.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Nethinims are the given ones: a body of temple servants, not of Israel by descent, appointed to the menial work of the house of God so that the Levites could attend to theirs. Their origin lies in two places. The Gibeonites were made “hewers of wood and drawers of water… for the house of my God” by Joshua; and Ezra records a later augmentation — “of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites” (Ezr 8:20). Their names in the registers are largely foreign. What matters is what happened to them. When Cyrus opened the way home, most of the exiles stayed in Babylon where they had houses and trades; and among the small company that went up were “all the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants… three hundred ninety and two” (Ezr 2:58). Slaves of the sanctuary walked back to a ruin to serve in it. They are listed with the priests and Levites as exempt from tribute by Artaxerxes' decree, they built their portion of the wall, they dwelt in Ophel by the water gate (Neh 3:26; Neh 11:21), and they sealed the covenant with Nehemiah. Descendants of the conquered, given to the house, and found at the door when the house was rebuilt.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Nethinims as servants of the priests and Levites in the temple, given or devoted to that service, chiefly of the Gibeonites and other captives.

expand to see more

NETHINIMS, n. plu. In Jewish antiquity, the servants of the priests and Levites in the temple.

The word signifies given or devoted, from a Hebrew verb to give.

They are supposed to have been the Gibeonites, made hewers of wood and drawers of water by Joshua.

David and the princes appointed others of them for the service of the Levites.

Many of them returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and with Ezra, and dwelt in Ophel.

Key Scripture

Ezr 2:58 — "All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two."

Ezr 8:20 — "Also of the Nethinims, whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites, two hundred and twenty Nethinims: all of them were expressed by name."

Neh 3:26 — "Moreover the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, unto the place over against the water gate toward the east, and the tower that lieth out."

Neh 11:21 — "But the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel: and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims."

Modern Corruption

An order of temple servants drawn from a conquered people is read as religious slavery; Scripture treats their inclusion as mercy and records their names, their exemption, and their voluntary return.

expand to see more

The Nethinims are sometimes cited as evidence that Israel's religion sanctified a caste system. The details will not support it. Under the law a foreigner attached to the sanctuary was protected, provided for, and brought within the covenant community — the Gibeonites, having lied their way to a treaty, were placed at the altar of the God they had feared, and four centuries later Saul's attempt to destroy them brought a three-year famine on Israel. Artaxerxes exempted the Nethinims from toll, tribute, and custom along with the priests. Ezra records them as “expressed by name”, which is the opposite of how a slave register is kept. And the covenant of Neh 10 is sealed by “the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God” — they are inside, by profession.

The principle to recover is what their name means. Nethinim is the passive of the verb “to give”: they are the given ones, men who did not give themselves but were given, and whose whole standing was that they belonged to the house. The New Testament says the same thing of the church in the words of Christ — “thine they were, and thou gavest them me” (Joh 17:6) — and of ministers, whom Paul calls “your servants for Jesus' sake” (2Co 4:5). Three hundred and ninety-two of them chose a ruined temple over a comfortable exile. That is what a given one looks like.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Nethinim (H5411), the given ones, from nathan (H5414), to give; compare nethunim (Num 8:16), the Levites “wholly given” to the LORD.

expand to see more

Hebrew Nethinim (H5411) — Nethinims; temple servants, literally those who have been given.

Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give, put, set; the root of the name and of Nathan, Jonathan, and Nethaniah.

Hebrew nethunim nethunim — “wholly given”; the doubled participle used of the Levites themselves (Num 8:16).

Hebrew 'Ophel (H6077) — Ophel, the swelling or hill south of the temple mount where they lived.

Hebrew chotebe 'etsim we-sho'abe mayim — hewers of wood and drawers of water; the Gibeonite office (Jos 9:23).

Usage

"“All the Nethinims… three hundred ninety and two” — the servants who came home."

"“Whom David and the princes had appointed for the service of the Levites” — an order with a charter."

"“The Nethinims dwelt in Ophel” — quarters beside the house they served."
